title: Introduction to allin1
text: important distinction. na.omit() drops row NA. drop_na_rows() drops rows every value missing, partially complete rows survive: base-R equivalent drop_na_rows() df[rowSums(.na(df)) < ncol(df), , drop = FALSE] — correct, verbose easy get wrong (forgetting drop = FALSE silently turns one-column result vector).
code: df <- data.frame(   name  = c("Alice", "Bob", NA),   score = c(10,       NA,    NA) )  # drop_na_rows() keeps Bob, he still has a name drop_na_rows(df) #>    name score #> 1 Alice    10 #> 2   Bob    NA  # na.omit() removes Bob too, just because his score is missing na.omit(df) #>    name score #> 1 Alice    10

title: Introduction to allin1
text: dplyr::slice_max() can take proportion, top_n_percent() lets think whole percentages returns exactly many rows rather expanding include ties: main motivation comes everyday problems data wrangling. People like often find quite tedious may make silly mistakes writing large chunks code like missing open pipe operator, missing parameter function. goal make shortcuts lengthy functions order create user-friendly data wrangling experience new experienced data scientists alike.
code: # dplyr: proportion as a fraction, and ties may add extra rows employees |> slice_max(hourly_wage, prop = 0.5)  # allin1: a plain percentage, exact row count employees |> top_n_percent(hourly_wage, percent = 50)
